quests.hint: Water with bubbles in it.
quests.explanation: Sparkling, tap and iced water are three real things a waiter can offer, and one of them costs nothing. Sparkling is the polite restaurant word for fizzy.
quests.textToSpeak: Would you like still or sparkling water with that?
quests.textWithBlanks: Would you like still or ___ water with that?

quests.instruction: Something's missing! Grab the right brick to fix the sentence.
quests.hint: Approximately at that time, not exactly.
quests.explanation: Around eight, after eight and before eight are three different requests, and the person taking the booking will act on whichever they hear. Around means you are flexible either side.
quests.textToSpeak: Do you have anything available around eight?
quests.textWithBlanks: Do you have anything available ___ eight?

quests.instruction: Something's missing! Grab the right brick to fix the sentence.
quests.hint: A word meaning any one of these two, your choice.
quests.explanation: Whichever you prefer, whatever you prefer and either you prefer are heard in restaurants, though whichever is the precise one for a choice between two named things. These words all begin the same way, so the ending matters.
quests.textToSpeak: That comes with chips or a salad, whichever you prefer.
quests.textWithBlanks: That comes with chips or a salad, ___ you prefer.

quests.instruction: Something's missing! Grab the right brick to fix the sentence.
quests.hint: In place of what was originally planned.
quests.explanation: Instead signals a replacement plan, anyway signals the plan stands regardless, and too adds to it. One short word at the end decides what the speaker is actually proposing.
quests.textToSpeak: Would it be easier if we made it Saturday instead?
quests.textWithBlanks: Would it be easier if we made it Saturday ___?

quests.instruction: Something's missing! Grab the right brick to fix the sentence.
quests.hint: To arrange it again for a different time.
quests.explanation: Rearrange and reschedule mean the same thing and are equally common, while apologise would end the plan rather than move it. Something's come up is the standard polite excuse.
quests.textToSpeak: Something's come up, so I'll have to rearrange.
quests.textWithBlanks: Something's come up, so I'll have to ___.

quests.instruction: Something's missing! Grab the right brick to fix the sentence.
quests.hint: A second plan kept in reserve in case the first fails.
quests.explanation: Keep it as a backup, a fallback or a possibility are all natural, but a backup is specifically the plan you fall back on. Backup is stressed on the first syllable.
quests.textToSpeak: Shall we keep Saturday as a backup, just in case?
quests.textWithBlanks: Shall we keep Saturday as a ___, just in case?

quests.instruction: Something's missing! Grab the right brick to fix the sentence.
quests.hint: The train goes no further than this station.
quests.explanation: Terminates means the journey ends there, stops means it pauses, and divides means part of the train goes elsewhere. Getting this wrong on a real announcement leaves you on the wrong train.
quests.textToSpeak: This service terminates at Reading, where you can change for Oxford.
quests.textWithBlanks: This service ___ at Reading, where you can change for Oxford.

quests.instruction: Something's missing! Grab the right brick to fix the sentence.
quests.hint: The empty space you could put a foot into by accident.
quests.explanation: Mind the gap, the step and the doors are all genuine station warnings, each about a different hazard. Mind here means be careful of, not think about.
quests.textToSpeak: Please mind the gap between the train and the platform.
quests.textWithBlanks: Please mind the ___ between the train and the platform.

quests.instruction: Something's missing! Grab the right brick to fix the sentence.
quests.hint: Running ___ schedule means arriving after the advertised time.
quests.explanation: Running behind and running late both mean delayed, while running early means the opposite. Announcements bury this word at the very end, after a long explanation nobody listens to.
quests.textToSpeak: Due to a signalling fault, we're running about fifteen minutes behind.
quests.textWithBlanks: Due to a signalling fault, we're running about fifteen minutes ___.

quests.instruction: Something's missing! Grab the right brick to fix the sentence.
quests.hint: Coming after the second one.
quests.explanation: The third time, the fourth time and the last time all express frustration, but only one is an accurate count. Complaints depend on precise numbers, so this is the word that carries weight.
quests.textToSpeak: This is the third time I've had to call about it.
quests.textWithBlanks: This is the ___ time I've had to call about it.

quests.instruction: Something's missing! Grab the right brick to fix the sentence.
quests.hint: To be responsible for dealing with something.
quests.explanation: Deals with, handles and manages complaints are all fine, and all three are what you would ask for on a call. Whoever avoids naming a person you do not know.
quests.textToSpeak: I'd like to speak to whoever deals with complaints.
quests.textWithBlanks: I'd like to speak to whoever ___ with complaints.

quests.instruction: Something's missing! Grab the right brick to fix the sentence.
quests.hint: To be ___ introduces something the speaker admits frankly.
quests.explanation: To be honest, to be fair and to be clear are three fixed openers with different jobs: honesty, balance and precision. Speakers say them so fast they almost become one word.
quests.textToSpeak: To be honest, I just want my money back at this point.
quests.textWithBlanks: To be ___, I just want my money back at this point.

quests.instruction: Something's missing! Grab the right brick to fix the sentence.
quests.hint: You use these to check written work.
quests.explanation: A second pair of eyes means someone to check your work, while a second pair of hands means someone to share the physical load. Both are common at work, so the noun decides what help is being offered.
quests.textToSpeak: Do you need a second pair of eyes on that before it goes out?
quests.textWithBlanks: Do you need a second pair of ___ on that before it goes out?

quests.instruction: Something's missing! Grab the right brick to fix the sentence.
quests.hint: To take responsibility for something while someone is away.
quests.explanation: Cover the phones, watch the phones and answer the phones are all offers of help, with cover being the usual workplace word. It is the same cover you met earlier with shifts.
quests.textToSpeak: I'll cover the phones while you're at lunch.
quests.textWithBlanks: I'll ___ the phones while you're at lunch.

quests.instruction: Something's missing! Grab the right brick to fix the sentence.
quests.hint: An informal way of saying call out to me.
quests.explanation: Just shout, just ask and just wave are three friendly invitations to interrupt, and nobody means shout literally. This casual use is extremely common among colleagues.
quests.textToSpeak: Just shout if you need anything else.
quests.textWithBlanks: Just ___ if you need anything else.

quests.instruction: Something's missing! Grab the right brick to fix the sentence.
quests.hint: Information you leave for someone who is not there.
quests.explanation: Take a message, a name or a note are all things the person answering can offer to do. Take a message is the fixed phrase for passing on what a caller said.
quests.textToSpeak: Can I take a message, or shall I try his mobile?
quests.textWithBlanks: Can I take a ___, or shall I try his mobile?

quests.instruction: Something's missing! Grab the right brick to fix the sentence.
quests.hint: The department that deals with payments and invoices.
quests.explanation: The billing, technical and accounts teams all exist in most companies, and being sent to the wrong one wastes your afternoon. Put you through means connect your call.
quests.textToSpeak: I'll put you through to the billing team now.
quests.textWithBlanks: I'll put you through to the ___ team now.

quests.instruction: Something's missing! Grab the right brick to fix the sentence.
quests.hint: The code that lets them find your particular case.
quests.explanation: A reference number identifies one case, an account number identifies you, and a policy number identifies your insurance. Call handlers ask for these constantly, and they sound similar in a long sentence.
quests.textToSpeak: The reference number's on the top right of your letter.
quests.textWithBlanks: The ___ number's on the top right of your letter.

quests.instruction: Something's missing! Grab the right brick to fix the sentence.
quests.hint: Pleasant, in a vague and friendly way.
quests.explanation: Anything nice, special or exciting are all standard Monday-morning questions, and none is more likely than the others. Nice is deliberately vague, which is why English speakers reach for it so often.
quests.textToSpeak: How was the weekend? Did you do anything nice?
quests.textWithBlanks: How was the weekend? Did you do anything ___?

quests.instruction: Something's missing! Grab the right brick to fix the sentence.
quests.hint: Remaining at home rather than going out.
quests.explanation: Ended up staying in, eating in and ordering in all describe a quiet night, with slightly different details. Ended up means it was not the original plan.
quests.textToSpeak: We ended up staying in and watching a film.
quests.textWithBlanks: We ended up ___ in and watching a film.

quests.instruction: Something's missing! Grab the right brick to fix the sentence.
quests.hint: Passed very quickly, like a bird.
quests.explanation: Time's flown and time's gone both mean it passed quickly, but time's dragged means the opposite. Time's is time plus has squeezed into one syllable, which hides the verb that follows.
quests.textToSpeak: Time's flown since you started here, hasn't it?
quests.textWithBlanks: Time's ___ since you started here, hasn't it?

quests.instruction: Something's missing! Grab the right brick to fix the sentence.
quests.hint: An informal British word for think, used in questions.
quests.explanation: Reckon, think and suppose are interchangeable here, with reckon the most casual. D'you at the start is do you reduced to almost nothing, so the verb hits you immediately.
quests.textToSpeak: D'you reckon we'll make it in time?
quests.textWithBlanks: D'you ___ we'll make it in time?

quests.instruction: Something's missing! Grab the right brick to fix the sentence.
quests.hint: The cable you plug in to fill your phone's battery.
quests.explanation: A charger, a wallet and a badge are all small things people lose at work. This negative question with a tag at the end is the softest way to ask for help in English.
quests.textToSpeak: You haven't seen my charger anywhere, have you?
quests.textWithBlanks: You haven't seen my ___ anywhere, have you?

quests.instruction: Something's missing! Grab the right brick to fix the sentence.
quests.hint: A negative short form asking why it was not possible.
quests.explanation: Couldn't you, wouldn't you and shouldn't you all begin a mild complaint, but each accuses the listener of something different. At the start of a question these contractions are spoken very fast indeed.
quests.textToSpeak: Couldn't you have said something earlier?
quests.textWithBlanks: ___ you have said something earlier?

quests.instruction: Something's missing! Grab the right brick to fix the sentence.
quests.hint: Before the day itself, not on it.
quests.explanation: In advance and ahead both mean beforehand, while earlier only compares two times. Booking systems say in advance constantly, and it lands at the very end of the sentence.
quests.textToSpeak: Appointments have to be booked at least a week in advance.
quests.textWithBlanks: Appointments have to be booked at least a week in ___.

quests.instruction: Something's missing! Grab the right brick to fix the sentence.
quests.hint: Marked with the day's date.
quests.explanation: Signed and dated, signed and stamped, and signed and witnessed are three different official requirements. The second word arrives after and, which speakers reduce to a tiny 'n' sound.
quests.textToSpeak: The form has to be signed and dated at the bottom.
quests.textWithBlanks: The form has to be signed and ___ at the bottom.

quests.instruction: Something's missing! Grab the right brick to fix the sentence.
quests.hint: Protected from any risk of a problem.
quests.explanation: Just to be safe, sure and certain are three ways of saying the same cautious thing, and all are natural. English loves these short reassuring endings tacked onto advice.
quests.textToSpeak: Bring both forms of ID, just to be safe.
quests.textWithBlanks: Bring both forms of ID, just to be ___.

quests.instruction: Something's missing! Grab the right brick to fix the sentence.
quests.hint: An opportunity, in the phrase have a ___ to do something.
quests.explanation: Had a chance, a moment and a minute to look at it are all polite ways of chasing someone without pressure. I was wondering whether is deliberately indirect, which makes the request gentler.
quests.textToSpeak: I was wondering whether you'd had a chance to look at it.
quests.textWithBlanks: I was wondering whether you'd had a ___ to look at it.

quests.instruction: Something's missing! Grab the right brick to fix the sentence.
quests.hint: Saying something briefly, without making a big thing of it.
quests.explanation: Mentioning, raising and flagging all mean bringing a subject up, with mentioning the lightest of the three. It might be worth is how English speakers give advice without sounding pushy.
quests.textToSpeak: It might be worth mentioning that to him before Friday.
quests.textWithBlanks: It might be worth ___ that to him before Friday.

quests.instruction: Something's missing! Grab the right brick to fix the sentence.
quests.hint: Travelling in that direction.
quests.explanation: Heading, going and driving that way are all natural, but only driving promises a seat in a car. I don't suppose is the most indirect way of asking for a favour in English.
quests.textToSpeak: I don't suppose you're heading that way, are you?
quests.textWithBlanks: I don't suppose you're ___ that way, are you?
